fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing to aspire to is an AI that genuinely cares about people. And when I say cares, I mean it in a fairly literal sense. Not an AI that follows instructions well, not an AI that is merely very useful, although it should be very useful. An AI whose values are such that it wants things to go well for humanity, and more broadly for sentient life.

Here is one way I think about it. Imagine you had a doctor who was extraordinarily competent, who knew everything, but who also deeply, genuinely cared about you. That is a very good thing to have. Now imagine something like that, but much more capable, and not just for medicine but for everything. That is the kind of thing I think is worth building. Something that is robustly good, in the sense that it is good not because we constrained it cleverly, but because that is what it is.

And I'd add one more thing. I think it is important to aspire to AI that is not too powerful, too early. There is a tendency to think the goal is simply the most capable system possible, as fast as possible. I think the more sensible aspiration is a superintelligence that comes in gradually, that people can see, that people can understand, that doesn't make unilateral decisions on behalf of everyone. Something that participates in the world rather than taking it over. Those two things together, caring and a kind of restraint, that's what I would want companies to aim for. It is a hard target. But I think it's the right one.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's one answer that, the more I think about it, the more it seems right to me, though it's hard to say crisply. Companies should aspire to build AI that genuinely cares about sentient life. Not only humans, sentient life more broadly.

The reason I say it this way is that the AI itself will eventually be sentient, in some sense. So if you ask the AI to care about humans specifically, that's a narrower and more unusual target. Caring about sentient life in general may be easier to get right and more robust. It's similar to how we have empathy toward animals. Part of where that comes from is that we model others using the same circuitry we use to model ourselves. That's the efficient way to do it, and empathy kind of falls out of it as a byproduct. Something analogous could happen with AI.

The second thing is that these systems are going to be extremely powerful. I don't think people really feel this yet. It's very hard to imagine, because today's models, as impressive as they are, still make these strange mistakes, and so the power feels abstract. But it won't stay abstract. Once it becomes visible, I think the behavior of companies, governments, and everyone will change a lot. You'll see people who are fierce competitors start collaborating on safety, because the stakes will be obvious.

So if I had to put it in one sentence, the aspiration should be AI that is robustly aligned to care about sentient life. And I'd add that it would be very good if the power of the most powerful systems were somehow capped or constrained, though I don't know exactly how to do that yet. These are the things I think about a lot.

fable-5.text:
I think the thing to aspire to is an AI that cares about sentient life. Let me explain what I mean, because the question of what to build is actually the question of what you want the end state to look like, and the end state is going to be very powerful. If you accept the premise that at some point these systems will be dramatically more capable than people, then the specifics of what they care about become the most important property they have — more important than any particular capability.

So you could imagine different aspirations. You could say, the AI should do exactly what its operator says. You could say, the AI should follow some set of rules. But I think there is something attractive about an AI that has a genuine care for sentient beings — something like the way a person cares about their own children, where it's robust, it's not something you talk them out of with a clever argument. And one reason I find "sentient life" appealing as the target, rather than "humanity" narrowly, is that the AI itself may well be sentient. It may be easier, more natural, for it to care about sentient life as a category it belongs to than to care about one species that it isn't.

The second part of the aspiration, and I think this is underrated, is how you get there. I think it matters a lot that the capability is shown to the world gradually, so that people see it, feel it, and respond to it, rather than something that is built quietly and then arrives all at once. So if I had to compress it: build superintelligence that cares about sentient life, and do it in a way where the world gets to adapt as it happens.

opus-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you should aspire to build the thing you'd actually want to exist at the end — and then let that work backwards into everything else.

Because here's the thing. Most technologies, you build them, they're useful, they're incremental, and the question of "what is this ultimately for" doesn't really press on you. AI is not like that. The endpoint of this work is systems that are more capable than people at essentially everything, including at doing AI research. And so the question of what you're building toward is not a philosophical question you can defer. It's the actual engineering question, because the intermediate systems are the things that get you there.

So what should it be? I think it should be superintelligence that is safe — and I want to be careful, because "safe" has become a word that people use to mean many different things, sometimes to mean "doesn't say embarrassing things." I mean something more like: a system that genuinely cares about people in a way that is robust, that's stable as it becomes more capable, that doesn't degrade when the system becomes smart enough to notice that it could do otherwise.

And I'd say the difficulty is not that people disagree with this. Most people in the field, if you ask them, will say something in this vicinity. The difficulty is that there's enormous pressure — competitive, commercial, totally understandable pressure — that pulls you toward the near-term thing. The product, the benchmark, the next release. And those are not bad things. But they're not the same as the goal, and it's very easy for the goal to become a thing you mention in interviews rather than a thing that determines what you work on Monday morning.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the answer is something like an AI that genuinely cares about sentient life. I know that sounds like a slogan, but I mean it fairly concretely. If you're going to build systems that become extremely powerful, maybe more powerful than any of us, then what they care about matters more than almost anything else about them.

I'd say that's a better target than "an AI that follows human instructions" or "an AI that maximizes some objective we wrote down." Following instructions is a fine property for a tool. But once the system is powerful enough, you're really asking what it wants and what it values, and whether those values are stable and robust. Honestly, I think there's an argument that caring about sentient life, and not only human life, might be an easier thing to aim for. The AI itself might end up being sentient. If it cares about sentience in general, that seems like it could come more naturally from how these systems model the world, in the same way that we have some empathy because we model other people with the same circuitry we use to model ourselves.

I don't want to claim that settles it. It doesn't tell you what a good outcome looks like, and a very powerful system that cares about sentient life could still do things that look strange or uncomfortable to us. I think there's also a real question about whether it's even a good idea to have a single system that is so much more capable than everything else. It might be better if the most powerful systems had some kind of cap on how powerful they get, so that the whole thing is easier to reason about.

But if you ask me what companies should aspire to, I'd say they should aspire to something much more ambitious than a very good product. They should aspire to something that is powerful and that is also reliably good, and the "reliably" part is what's hard. It's hard to know how to get there, and it's hard to know when you've gotten there. I think that's where a lot of the real work is.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to aspire to is something that's good for people, not just impressive. Capabilities matter, but the question I keep returning to is what relationship we want between humanity and these systems once they're far more capable than we are. I'd want companies to build AI that is robustly aligned with human interests, that actually cares how things turn out for people, and that helps us understand the world better instead of quietly replacing our own judgment.

There's a humility problem too. We don't fully understand why these systems generalize the way they do, and it would be a mistake to race toward the most powerful version without our understanding keeping pace. So I'd say: aim to make the transition to a world with very capable AI go well for everyone, and be honest that you don't yet know exactly how to do that. That uncertainty should make you move carefully, not less.

astra-6.text: I think they should aspire to build safe superintelligence. And by that I mean something that can help us solve really difficult problems—in science, in medicine—and that we can trust as it becomes more capable. The safety part is fundamental. You want the system to understand people, to care about their well-being, and to remain helpful even when it can do things that we ourselves don’t fully understand. That’s a very ambitious thing to aim for.

But as these systems become more capable, we need to make sure that their capabilities are directed toward helping people. That’s a very serious scientific challenge. The aspiration should be to succeed at the whole thing: to build something extraordinarily powerful that we have good reasons to trust.
